paragraphs.heading: The statement
paragraphs.text: Fermat's little theorem is a fact about primes. Pick a prime number p and any integer a; then aᵖ − a is a whole-number multiple of p. In the shorthand of modular arithmetic this reads aᵖ ≡ a (mod p). With a = 2 and p = 7, for instance, 2⁷ = 128, and 128 − 2 = 126 = 7 × 18. The theorem underlies the Fermat primality test and counts among the fundamental results of elementary number theory.

paragraphs.heading: A second form
paragraphs.text: If p does not divide a, so that a is coprime to p, the theorem can be put another way: aᵖ⁻¹ − 1 is a multiple of p, or aᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p). Using the same numbers, 2⁶ = 64, and 64 − 1 = 63 = 7 × 9.

paragraphs.heading: Name and history
paragraphs.text: The theorem carries the name of Pierre de Fermat, who stated it in 1640. It is called little to tell it apart from Fermat's Last Theorem. Fermat added that he would send a demonstration if he were not afraid of going on too long. Euler published the first proof in 1736, though Leibniz had given nearly the same proof in an unpublished manuscript from before 1683.

paragraphs.heading: A test that can be fooled
paragraphs.text: Some mathematicians guessed that 2ᵖ ≡ 2 (mod p) holds exactly when p is prime. Half of this is right: for a prime p it follows as one particular instance of Fermat's little theorem. The other half fails. The number 341 = 11 × 31 is not prime, yet 2³⁴¹ ≡ 2 (mod 341), so it is called a pseudoprime to base 2. Pierre Frédéric Sarrus found this first one in 1820.

paragraphs.heading: Part of a bigger theorem
paragraphs.text: The theorem is often proved as a consequence of Euler's theorem. That result uses Euler's totient function φ(n), which counts how many integers between 1 and n are coprime to n. Fermat's little theorem is the special case where n is prime, because then φ(n) = n − 1.

paragraphs.heading: Locks on messages
paragraphs.text: Euler's theorem, used with an n that is not prime, is at work in public-key cryptography, notably the RSA system. Using public values n and e, a message x becomes y = xᵉ (mod n). Anyone who knows φ(n) can find the integer f with ef ≡ 1 (mod φ(n)) using the extended Euclidean algorithm, and then recover x ≡ y^f (mod n). With what is known today, decrypting without the secret factors p and q of n is not possible.
